newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian mourns death of director Ferreri.
newsitem.headline: Italian mourns death of director Ferreri.

text.p: Italy mourned the passing of another of its cinema greats on Friday after director Marco Ferreri died of a heart attack in a Paris hospital aged 69.

Ferreri made more than 30 films, delving into folly and perversion in pictures like his 1973 satire "La Grande Bouffe" about a group of wealthy friends who literally ate and drunk themselves to death in an orgiastic blow-out.

"He was a courageous intellectual and his films were among the most ironic and original in the history of cinema," Culture Minister Walter Veltroni said in a telegram to the director's wife, Jacqueline.
"This is the loss of a very important man for Italian culture and cinema, of an extraordinary personality and of a great director," he added.
Ferreri had an electic and anarchic style, often tinged with a deep sarcasm towards what he saw as the self-destructing values of consumer society.

The hero of his first English-language feature (Bye Bye Monkey, 1978) gets gang-raped by a group of women, while the 1991 film "La Carne" (Flesh) was a lurid tale of a love so obsessive that it culminates with the man killing his girlfriend, storing her in the fridge and eating her.
Italian actress and sex symbol Francesca Dellera, who had a leading role in "La Carne", said she owed everything to the director.
"I am saddened because working with him was the high point of my career, but also because he was an incredibly sensitive person who helped me in a tough moment in my life," she said.
One of Ferreri's best known films was his 1969 masterpiece "Dillinger Is Dead," a darkly moody allegory on the breakup of marriage starring French actor Michel Piccoli.
Piccoli, who is starring in a play in the Italian city of Genoa, was reported to have locked himself in his dressing room in grief at his friend's death before taking the stage later on Friday.

"His power as director and artist came from the way he interpreted the world in his own, very personal way," Italian director Marco Bellocchio was quoted as saying at the Cannes Film Festival. "It was immediately recognisable and poetic."
The Milan-born Ferreri, who made his first feature films in Spain, was a close friend of actor and compatriot Marcello Mastroianni and the two were neighbours in Paris's Latin Quarter.
"Mastroianni is not dead -- men like Marcello do not die," Ferreri said last December after the 72-year-old star of "La Dolce Vita" (The Sweet Life) died of cancer.
Mastroianni played alongside his French lover Catherine Deneuve in Ferreri's films "La Cagna" (The Bitch), "La Grande Bouffe" and "Liza".
Ferreri once said the cinema was a place where society could forget its divisions.
"The cinema has always been a place open to everyone," he said. "When the cinema arrived, for a few cents, people who were rich or poor finally found themselves laughing and crying together."
Gilles Jacob, supremo of the Cannes film festival, said: "The Italian cinema has lost one of its most original artists, one of its most personal authors.

"No one was more demanding nor more allegorical than he in showing the state of crisis of contemporary man. The Cannes film festival, which screened eight of his films and gave three of them prizes, will not forget him."
